meta.title: Secure SDLC Gap Checker
meta.note: A maturity rubric grounded in NIST SSDF (SP 800-218) and OWASP SAMM. Leverage and friction ratings are practitioner guidance to sequence adoption, not a certification.

sources.name: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)

practices.name: Threat modeling
practices.why: Finding design flaws before code is written is far cheaper than patching them in production, and it surfaces the abuse cases a feature spec usually skips.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Designs ship with no structured look at how a feature could be attacked.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: A senior engineer occasionally sketches threats for a big feature, informally and inconsistently.

levels.label: Repeatable
levels.detail: New or changed high-risk features get a lightweight threat model using a shared template.

levels.label: Integrated
levels.detail: Threat models are a required, tracked design-review step with owners and follow-up on mitigations.

practices.engineerNote: You run a 30-minute template-driven session only on features touching auth, data, or trust boundaries, so most changes are untouched.

practices.name: Security requirements
practices.why: Writing security expectations (authz, data handling, logging) into the spec up front prevents the vague, expensive rework that happens when they surface during review or an audit.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Requirements cover features and performance but say nothing about security or data handling.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Security needs come up verbally in reviews, depending on who is in the room.

levels.label: Standardized
levels.detail: A reusable checklist of security and privacy requirements is attached to relevant stories.

levels.label: Traceable
levels.detail: Security requirements are tracked to acceptance criteria and verified before release.

practices.engineerNote: You pull from a short pre-written checklist during design instead of inventing requirements later, which removes surprise rework at review time.

practices.name: Secrets management
practices.why: Keeping credentials out of code and config and in a managed store limits the blast radius when a repo, laptop, or log leaks, which is one of the most common breach paths.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Passwords, keys, and tokens live hardcoded in source or checked-in config.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Some secrets move to environment variables or local files, handled per team.

levels.label: Centralized
levels.detail: Secrets live in a managed vault or secrets manager, injected at runtime.

levels.label: Governed
levels.detail: Secrets are centrally stored, access-scoped, rotated, and audited automatically.

practices.engineerNote: You reference a secret by name from a vault client instead of pasting values, so local runs and deploys get the right credential without you tracking it.

practices.name: Secure coding standards
practices.why: Agreed patterns for input handling, output encoding, and error handling stop the same avoidable bug classes (injection, unsafe deserialization) from recurring across teams.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Each engineer decides how to handle input, auth, and errors on their own.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Some tribal knowledge and scattered wiki notes exist but nothing is agreed or enforced.

levels.label: Documented
levels.detail: A language-specific secure coding guide with paved-road patterns is published and referenced.

levels.label: Reinforced
levels.detail: Standards are backed by linters, shared libraries, and templates so the safe path is the default.

practices.engineerNote: The safe patterns ship as linter rules and shared helpers, so you follow the standard by using the paved road, not by memorizing a document.

practices.name: Security code review
practices.why: A human eye on security-relevant changes catches logic and authorization flaws that automated scanners miss, especially in auth, access control, and money-handling paths.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Code merges with no security-focused review beyond normal functional review.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Reviewers flag security issues occasionally when they happen to notice them.

levels.label: Guided
levels.detail: Security-sensitive changes get a review using a shared checklist of what to look for.

levels.label: Assured
levels.detail: High-risk paths require a reviewer with security context, and coverage is tracked.

practices.engineerNote: Only changes touching sensitive paths trigger the extra security lens, so routine pull requests move at their normal pace.

practices.name: Static application security testing (SAST)
practices.why: Scanning source for known-dangerous patterns catches injection, unsafe APIs, and similar bug classes early, when they are cheap to fix and still in the author's head.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: No automated analysis of source for security-relevant defects.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: An engineer runs a scanner locally now and then and reads the output manually.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: SAST runs on every pull request and posts findings automatically.

levels.label: Tuned
levels.detail: Rules are tuned for low noise, high-severity findings block merge, and results are triaged.

practices.engineerNote: It runs in the background on your pull request and only blocks on a small tuned set of high-confidence, high-severity findings, not style noise.

practices.name: SCA dependency scanning
practices.why: Most application code is third-party dependencies, so scanning them for known vulnerabilities catches a large share of real risk with almost no effort from engineers.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Nobody tracks which open-source versions are pulled in or whether they have known CVEs.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Dependencies get checked manually before a big release or during an audit.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Every build scans dependencies against a vulnerability database and reports findings.

levels.label: Managed
levels.detail: Findings are prioritized by reachability and severity, with SLAs and auto-update pull requests.

practices.engineerNote: It flags vulnerable packages on your pull request and often opens the upgrade for you, so patching is a review, not a research project.

practices.name: Secret scanning in CI
practices.why: Automatically catching committed keys and tokens before they merge prevents the very common and costly mistake of a live credential landing in git history.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Nothing checks commits for accidentally committed credentials.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Secrets are caught only when a person happens to spot them in review.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: CI scans every commit and pull request for secret patterns and alerts on hits.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Detected secrets block the merge and trigger a defined rotation and revocation process.

practices.engineerNote: It only fires on a real detected credential, so a clean pull request never even sees it, and a hit tells you exactly what to rotate.

practices.name: Infrastructure as code scanning
practices.why: Checking Terraform, Kubernetes, and similar definitions before apply catches risky misconfigurations (open storage, permissive rules) while they are still a code change, not a live incident.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Infrastructure definitions merge and deploy with no security checks.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Someone occasionally eyeballs a config for obvious mistakes before applying it.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Every infra change is scanned against misconfiguration policies in the pipeline.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: High-severity misconfigurations block the apply, with documented exceptions and owners.

practices.engineerNote: It checks your infra change against clear policies in CI, so you learn about an open bucket or wide-open rule before it ships, not after.

practices.name: Software bill of materials (SBOM)
practices.why: A generated inventory of everything shipped lets you answer within minutes which builds contain a newly disclosed vulnerable component, instead of scrambling for days.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: There is no reliable list of what components and versions ship in a build.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Someone assembles a component list by hand when a customer or auditor asks.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: The pipeline generates a standard-format SBOM for each build automatically.

levels.label: Operationalized
levels.detail: SBOMs are stored, queryable, and wired into incident response for fast impact analysis.

practices.engineerNote: The build produces the SBOM for you as an artifact, so it costs you nothing at commit time and pays off the day a new CVE lands.

practices.name: Dynamic application security testing (DAST)
practices.why: Exercises a running application the way an attacker would, catching injection, auth, and configuration flaws that only appear at runtime and slip past static analysis.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: No dynamic testing; running app is never probed for security flaws.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Occasional manual scans, usually before a big release or an audit.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: A DAST scan runs against a staging deploy on a schedule or per release.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Scans gate promotion, findings have owners, and false positives are tuned out.

practices.engineerNote: DAST runs against a deployed staging environment on its own schedule, so it reports findings out of band rather than blocking your commits or pull requests.

practices.name: Container image vulnerability scanning
practices.why: Most container risk lives in the base image and OS packages you inherited, not your code; scanning surfaces known-vulnerable layers before they ship to production.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Images ship without any check for known-vulnerable OS or library layers.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Someone scans an image manually now and then, results not tracked.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Every image build is scanned automatically and results are recorded.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Builds fail on new critical or high findings, with a documented exception path.

practices.engineerNote: Scanning hooks into the image build you already run, adds a few seconds, and points you at a base-image bump rather than asking you to rewrite anything.

practices.name: Security regression and abuse-case tests
practices.why: Turns each fixed vulnerability and known abuse case into an automated test so the same bug cannot quietly return in a later change.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: No automated tests target abuse cases or previously fixed security bugs.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: A few security tests exist but are written inconsistently and rarely added.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Security and abuse-case tests run in CI alongside the normal test suite.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Every security fix ships with a regression test, tracked as part of done.

practices.engineerNote: These are ordinary unit and integration tests in your existing suite, so they run at normal test speed and fail loudly the moment a fixed issue reappears.

practices.name: Artifact signing and build provenance
practices.why: Signing artifacts and recording how they were built lets you prove that what runs in production is what your pipeline actually produced, closing off tampering and supply-chain swaps.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Artifacts are unsigned and there is no record of how they were built.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Some artifacts are signed manually or inconsistently, provenance is informal.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: The pipeline signs artifacts and generates provenance on every build.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Deploys verify signatures and provenance, and unsigned artifacts are rejected.

practices.engineerNote: Signing and provenance run automatically at build time in CI, so once the signing keys and trust root are set up, your day-to-day commit and review flow does not change.

practices.name: CI/CD pipeline hardening
practices.why: The pipeline holds credentials and pushes straight to production, so least-privilege CI, protected branches, no long-lived secrets, and pinned actions remove one of the highest-value attacker targets.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Broad CI tokens, long-lived secrets, unpinned actions, and unprotected branches.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Some controls exist on a few repos but nothing is applied consistently.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Least-privilege credentials, protected branches, and pinned actions are the default.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Policy enforces short-lived credentials and pinned actions across all repos, with drift alerts.

practices.engineerNote: This is mostly config on the pipeline you already have (short-lived tokens, pinned actions, branch protection), so it tightens security without touching how you write or ship code.

practices.name: Production deployment gates
practices.why: Change control on production deploys gives a clear approval and audit trail for what reaches users, so risky changes get a second look and every release is traceable.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Anyone can push to production with no approval or record of the change.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Approvals happen informally over chat and are not consistently recorded.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: The pipeline requires a defined approval step and logs who deployed what.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Risk-based gates and required approvers are enforced with a full, auditable trail.

practices.engineerNote: Gates are risk-scoped so routine low-risk changes flow through automatically, and approvals live in the pipeline rather than in a separate ticketing detour.

practices.name: Runtime security monitoring and alerting
practices.why: Logging and alerting on security-relevant events in production is how you notice an attack or abuse in progress instead of learning about it from a customer or a breach report.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: No logging or alerting on authentication, access, or other security events.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Some events are logged but nobody watches them and there are no alerts.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: Security events are logged centrally and alert on defined suspicious patterns.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Alerts route to an owner with response runbooks, and coverage is reviewed regularly.

practices.engineerNote: This builds on the logging and metrics stack you already run; you emit a few security-relevant events and the alerting is configured once, not per feature.

practices.name: Vulnerability disclosure and remediation SLA
practices.why: A published intake path plus a severity-based remediation SLA means outside reports reach the right team and get fixed on a predictable clock instead of sitting in an inbox.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: No way for anyone to report a vulnerability and no target for fixing one.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Reports trickle in through personal email with no owner or timeline.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: A published intake path routes reports to an owner with SLA targets by severity.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: SLA adherence is tracked and reported, and misses are escalated and reviewed.

practices.engineerNote: For engineers this is mostly a documented intake path and severity clock, so reports arrive as triaged, prioritized work rather than surprise fire drills.

practices.name: Automated dependency updates
practices.why: Most exploited vulnerabilities are known and already patched upstream; automating updates keeps you close to current so patching does not depend on someone remembering to check.

levels.label: None
levels.detail: Dependencies are updated only manually, usually long after a fix is available.

levels.label: Ad hoc
levels.detail: Updates happen occasionally when someone notices, with no regular cadence.

levels.label: Automated
levels.detail: A bot opens dependency update pull requests on a regular schedule.

levels.label: Enforced
levels.detail: Updates auto-merge when tests pass, and security patches meet a defined timeline.

practices.engineerNote: A tool like Dependabot or Renovate opens small, pre-tested pull requests that auto-merge when your CI is green, so patching becomes a quick review instead of manual chasing.
